title: May 2025 CPI: 0.1% on the month and core 0.1%, as goods prices stay flat
summary: Consumer prices rose 0.1 percent in May after 0.2 percent in April, and 2.4 percent over 12 months, up from 2.3 percent. Core rose 0.1 percent (2.8 percent over the year). Shelter rose 0.3 percent and was the main driver; energy fell 1.0 percent as gasoline fell; airline fares, vehicles and apparel declined, and core goods were unchanged.

source.title: Consumer Price Index — May 2025
source.timezone_note: In June, Eastern Time is Eastern Daylight Time, UTC−04:00, so the release time is 12:30 UTC.

overview: The headline index rose 0.1 percent seasonally adjusted, with shelter's 0.3 percent rise 'the primary factor'. Food rose 0.3 percent, with food at home and food away from home both up 0.3 percent. Energy fell 1.0 percent as seasonally adjusted gasoline fell 2.6 percent (−0.7 percent before adjustment); electricity rose 0.9 percent and natural gas fell 1.0 percent.

Core prices rose 0.1 percent after 0.2 percent. Medical care rose 0.3 percent, motor vehicle insurance 0.7 percent, personal care 0.5 percent and household furnishings and operations 0.3 percent, after 1.0 percent in April. Airline fares fell 2.7 percent, after falls of 2.8 percent in April and 5.3 percent in March; used cars and trucks fell 0.5 percent, new vehicles 0.3 percent and apparel 0.4 percent. Core goods were unchanged on the month.

The 12-month headline rose to 2.4 percent from 2.3 percent even though the monthly pace slowed, because a 12-month change depends on the month leaving the window as well as the one entering it. Core rose 2.8 percent over 12 months, the same as in March and April.

key_facts.label: Core, 12 months
key_facts.basis: Not seasonally adjusted; unchanged from the 12 months to March and to April

key_facts.label: Shelter
key_facts.basis: 'The primary factor' in the monthly increase, per the release

key_facts.label: Core goods
key_facts.basis: Commodities less food and energy commodities, Table A

channels.title: Soft core and the policy path (shorter maturities)
channels.source_fact: Core +0.1 percent on the month, the second 0.1 percent reading in three months; core 2.8 percent over 12 months.
channels.interpretation: Another soft monthly core reading supports the view that inflation is moving toward target, which would tend to bring expected cuts forward and lower shorter yields if investors took it at face value.

channels.title: Little goods pass-through (all maturities)
channels.source_fact: Core goods unchanged; new vehicles −0.3 percent, apparel −0.4 percent; household furnishings +0.3 percent after +1.0 percent.
channels.interpretation: Readers looking for import-cost pass-through find little of it in May's goods prices, which would ease concern about goods inflation and lower inflation compensation. One month without pass-through does not rule it out later.

channels.title: A 12-month uptick that is arithmetic (longer maturities)
channels.source_fact: The 12-month headline rose to 2.4 percent from 2.3 percent while the monthly pace slowed to 0.1 percent.
channels.interpretation: A reader focused on the 12-month headline might see a slight re-acceleration; the monthly figures show the uptick comes from the comparison month, not new pressure. As a signal for inflation compensation, this channel is weak.

competing_explanations.title: Softness from volatile items
competing_explanations.detail: Airline fares, used cars and new vehicles carry much of the core softness, and these are volatile. Discounting them leaves a less soft picture of underlying inflation.

competing_explanations.title: Services excluding shelter still firm
competing_explanations.detail: Motor vehicle insurance (+0.7 percent), personal care (+0.5 percent) and medical care (+0.3 percent) kept rising. A reader focused on services would see persistence that the 0.1 percent core figure hides.

competing_explanations.title: Seasonal adjustment in energy
competing_explanations.detail: Seasonally adjusted gasoline fell 2.6 percent against 0.7 percent unadjusted, so part of the soft headline reflects seasonal factors rather than price changes investors would extrapolate.

assumptions: Investors read goods prices as the test of import-cost pass-through and services as the test of persistence.
A soft month adds to a trend rather than standing alone, given March's similar core reading.
Policy at the time was sensitive at the margin to inflation data.
missing_information: A sourced, contemporaneous consensus for headline and core CPI. Without it this case cannot say whether the release was a surprise.
Unrounded monthly changes; core at 0.1 and 0.2 percent may differ by very little before rounding.
Import price data or import shares by category, which would show whether flat goods prices mean no pass-through or offsetting moves.
The personal consumption expenditures price index for May, published later; not used.
weakening_observations: If goods prices rose sharply in the following months, May's flat reading would look like a lull before pass-through rather than its absence.
If the seasonal factors updated in February 2026 materially changed May's adjusted figures, readings of the monthly changes would weaken; this case does not check revised values.
If a sourced consensus had expected similar figures, the policy-path channel would be close to inactive for this release.

critique.title: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence
critique.detail: The case notes little goods pass-through in May. One flat month does not show that pass-through will not happen, and the case should not be read as a conclusion about the effects of trade policy.

critique.title: Two soft months in three is a short streak
critique.detail: Core rose 0.1, 0.2 and 0.1 percent in March, April and May. Calling that a trend leans on rounded tenths over three observations; the case should be careful about extrapolating it.

critique.title: Headline and 12-month signals disagree
critique.detail: The monthly headline slowed while the 12-month rate rose. The case explains why, but a reader skimming the summary could take away either message; the analysis would be clearer leading with the monthly figures.

critique.title: Third of four, read later
critique.detail: The third of four consecutive CPI releases in the library, included by that rule and analysed in October 2026 by an AI assistant that may know how goods prices behaved later in 2025. The case avoids that knowledge, but it may still shape how the pass-through channel is framed.

source_notes.title: Text used
source_notes.detail: The archived release as published, which shows 'Last Modified Date: June 11, 2025'. Figures come from the release text and Table A.

source_notes.title: Seasonal-factor revisions
source_notes.detail: BLS updates CPI seasonal factors each February and revises the previous five years of seasonally adjusted data, as its June 2025 release states. The monthly changes here are as first published; later revised values are not checked.

source_notes.title: Chained CPI
source_notes.detail: The release notes that chained CPI (C-CPI-U) indexes for the past 10 to 12 months are subject to revision. This case does not use them.

provenance.method: Read the archived May 2025 CPI release on 2026-10-05, and the archived June 2025 CPI release for its statement of the seasonal-revision schedule. Facts come from the release text and Table A; the channels, competing explanations and critique are the assistant's interpretation. No market prices, forecasts, surveys or news coverage were used.
